But I'd also argue that quite a few other MMORPGs fall into this category as well.

City of Heroes/Villains didn't have a main quest line... You got a new contact, and as you completed the missions they gave you, you'd slowly learn more about whatever little story arc you were participating in. Some were really short - only a few missions long - and some took you from one contact to another, culminating in a confrontation with some big supervillain/hero.

Does World of Warcraft really have a main questline? It doesn't seem like it to me, but I could be missing something. It seems like the war between the Alliance and the Horde isn't so much of a questline, but rather a premise for whatever quests you might currently be doing.

But a single-player open-world RPG without a main questline... That's definitely rarer. Can't really think of one, TBH. I don't think I would be put off by it, though, as long as the 'sidequests' (I guess without a main quest, they'd just be called 'quests') were engaging and interesting.

What actually makes a main quest line, though? If we look at Skyrim, everyone agrees that the quest line to kill Alduin is the main quest. But, why? Because Bethesda said so? I propose that (in the Elder Scrolls games specifically) that because of the non-linear progression, there is no "main quest line", but instead has a really long quest line. As long as the game is non-linear, you only have a main quest line when the developers state that it is the main quest line.

To look at Skyrim again, after escaping Helgen, you are completely free to do whatever you want. Since the Dragons don't actually spawn until after you speak to the jarl of Whiterun, you can actually do multiple quest lines before even starting the main quest. A friend of mine actually did the Thiefs Guild and Dark Brotherhood quest lines before starting the main quest. At that point, is it really a main quest? That's what Bethesda say, but in a completely non-linear world, I beg to question the existence of a main quest.

Meanwhile, if you look at a game like The Witcher 2, there is a set progression of the main story. The side quests are seen more like tasks than actual quest lines. Each "town" has a defined start and finish. They have made it so while the game is quite linear, it feels non-linear. But, it's quite linear and therefore does have a main quest line.
Absolutely. You could get literally hundreds of hours of content from Skyrim without ever touching the 'main quest'. The real main quest is whatever you make it.

Mount & Blade Warband is an open-world RPG and it is very free-form. The "main" quest is to become King and re-unite the continent but that's only one goal you can have. It has no real story to speak of either, except your own. Quests are randomly generated.

Quest lines that intersect in some way (be it order in which they are done, characters met, reputation of player to factions, etc). It would be neat if you can craft your own "main" storyline that doesn't seemed canned.

Trials of Ascension tried to do that. It was to be an open world where players dictated the quests. Everything was to be player run. If there was a guy giving out gold for bringing him 10 wolf heads, it was because there was a player whose sheep flock was being hunted by wolves in the area who wanted them dead. If the king puts out a reward for killing an evil wizard, it is a player wizard that is being a nuisance to the kingdom and the player king wants him dead. It was a really good idea that just failed to obtain critical mass. It is currently being redone in a less ambitious way at Trials of Ascension: Exile.

I would be cautiously curious. I'd love to see a game like that. But on the other hand, it'll be hard as fuck to pull off. TES and Fallout 3+ shows how it can fail, in that beyond some canned responses from a few NPCs, the effects of the players adventures rarely had any impact on the world.

Like in Skyrim, you join a civil war, but the impact is fairly minimal, from what I remember. There are mods that add more stuff for the civil war into it, but it's still not great.

It doesn't have to be huge sweeping changes. Say, you freed a bunch of slaves, and now there's a lot more labourers in cities as they seek employment. Or clearing out a mine allows a town to prosper, and their standard of living increases, and have better goods to sell. Stuff like that. Just something more then canned responses.

But, like I said, that's hard as hell to pull off.
